p.title: Feasibility of Big Data Analytics to Assess Personality Based on Voice Analysis

ext.title: Feasibility of Big Data Analytics to Assess Personality Based on Voice Analysis
ext.venue: Sensors 24(22), 7151 (MDPI, Basel). Received 30 Sep 2024; accepted 4 Nov 2024; published 7 Nov 2024. Open access, CC BY 4.0.
ext.document_type: Journal article (empirical, exploratory correlational and classification study)
ext.coverage: Whole file read: all 1517 lines of C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\557f30945d46.txt in two chunks (lines 1-1073, then 1074-1517), covering abstract, introduction, methods, results with Tables 3-6, discussion, limitations, supplementary note, and all 62 references. Metadata hint was correct; the venue field is confirmed as Sensors 24(22), 7151.
ext.research_question: Three questions stated on p.5 (Introduction, lines 266-286): (1) Are there voice features related to self-reported Big Five scores (externalization)? (2) Are the voice features related to externalization the same as those related to the accuracy of close-other and expert judgments? (3) Can personality dimensions be predicted from voice recorded with ordinary devices in controlled but not restricted speech, so the approach could fit Asynchronous Video Interviews and personnel selection?
ext.theory: Brunswick lens model as adapted by Scherer (1978): traits are externalized through objectively measurable speech variables (distal cues), perceived by listeners as proximal cues that ground attributions (p.2, lines 80-86). Brown and Bradshaw (1985) three facets: accuracy, externalization, attribution; this study tests externalization and accuracy (p.5, lines 258-265). Big Five framework; the authors also draw on the Cannata et al. (2022) call to join psychological personality-judgment research and personality computing (p.3, lines 156-163). Authors argue speech reveals the self (Allport and Cantril 1934; Allport 1937) (p.5, lines 238-239). No formal hypothesis is stated; the authors describe the study as exploratory.
ext.data: Unit: individual participant (interview recording). N = 100 female participants, split into Sample 1 (n = 78 female psychology students, aged 18-27, M = 20.18) and Sample 2 (n = 44 female participants, aged 18-54, M = 29.42) (p.5, lines 289-292). NOTE: the two sample sizes sum to 122, not 100; the text does not reconcile this. Recruitment: the first author's School of Psychology participant pool at Universidad Autonoma de Madrid, students paid in extra credit (p.5, lines 296-299). Recording period: not stated; the only date is the IRB approval of June 2016 (p.17, lines 1311-1313). Procedure: group session (60-item NEO-FFI, Spanish adaptation), individual interview in the following two weeks, about 7 min per session (p.7, lines 402-410). Audio: WAV, 16 kHz, mono, 16-bit; manually selected open-answer segments, mean 172.8 s (SD 102 s), range 49 s to 15 min; total 4 h 48 min (p.7, lines 414-430). Two different microphones were used for Sample 1 and Sample 2 (p.16). Data available only on request, for privacy reasons (p.17, line 1315). Expert rating subset: N = 20 videos for inter-rater ICC (p.7).
ext.method: Voice features: the AVEC 2011 emotion feature set extracted with OpenSMILE 2.3, 1941 features (25 energy/spectral LLDs x 42 functionals, 6 voicing LLDs x 32, 25 delta energy/spectral x 23, 6 delta voicing x 19, 10 voiced/unvoiced durations) (p.6, lines 311-323). Analysis 1 (externalization and accuracy): Pearson-type correlation of all 1941 features with each Big Five score from three criteria (self-report, close-other rubric, expert VAS), then reporting the top features per trait in Sample 1 (Table 4). Replication: the top-correlated self-report feature per trait was re-examined in Sample 2 (Section 3.1.6). Analysis 2 (prediction): for each of five traits, the five highest-correlated features were used; scores were binned into low/medium/high at the 25th and 75th percentiles of training data; random forest classifier (scikit-learn, n_estimators = 20, other defaults); leave-one-out with 100 folds (99 train / 1 test). SVM and multiple linear regression were tried but not reported because random forests did better (p.13, lines 1005-1010). Software: Python with Pandas, SciPy, scikit-learn (p.8). The text does not say whether the five features were selected inside each LOO fold or on the full sample; this is a reviewer note, not a stated fact, and it bears on whether the reported accuracies are out-of-sample. The text also does not name the correlation type or any multiple-comparison correction across 1941 features.
ext.scope: Population: adult female Spanish participants recruited at one Madrid university; Sample 1 is mostly students aged 18-27. Institution: Universidad Autonoma de Madrid (School of Psychology and Polytechnic School of Engineering). Era: collection date not stated; published 2024. Setting: semi-structured interview simulating a job interview (warm-up questions, then self-description, career, and a 15-year future question; p.7 lines 418-424). Sex: all participants are female, which the authors treat as a sample restriction (p.16). Constructs: Big Five self-report, close-other judgments, and zero-acquaintance expert ratings from video plus audio.

key_findings.finding: Close-other ratings correlate with self-report on all Big Five dimensions except Openness. Expert ratings match self-report only for Conscientiousness and Extraversion.
key_findings.numbers: Close-other vs self, significant range 0.32 (Neuroticism) to 0.51 (Extraversion). Expert vs self: 'Responsibility' 0.34 and Extraversion 0.31; both significant, the rest not.

key_findings.finding: Single voice features correlate moderately with personality ratings in Sample 1. The top correlation per trait and criterion is given in Table 4.
key_findings.numbers: Self: Extraversion 0.47 (mfcc_sma[3]_lpgain), Neuroticism 0.37, Openness 0.36, Agreeableness -0.33, Conscientiousness 0.30. Experts: Extraversion 0.48, Neuroticism -0.47, Conscientiousness 0.44, Openness -0.36, Agreeableness 0.35. Close others: Openness -0.41, Agreeableness -0.41, Neuroticism 0.32, Extraversion 0.40 (text says 0.40 in one sentence and 0.41 in the next), Conscientiousness -0.30.

key_findings.finding: Expert ratings showed the strongest voice correlates; the authors read this as expert judgments tracking voice cues more than close-other judgments do.
key_findings.numbers: Largest correlations with acoustic features came from the non-acquainted expert. Expert Extraversion accuracy 60% was the best prediction cell (Table 6).

key_findings.finding: The feature-level correlations did not replicate across samples. Sample 2 (self-report only) gave different features, although of similar magnitude.
key_findings.numbers: Sample 2 top features: Neuroticism mfcc_sma[1]_percentile99.0 r=0.52; Extraversion F0final_sma_quartile3 r=0.46 (p=0.002); Openness mfcc_sma[3]_kurtosis r=0.52; Agreeableness mfcc_sma[2]_skewness r=-0.46 (p=0.002); Conscientiousness mfcc_sma_de[7]_kurtosis r=-0.53. Authors say the results 'did not coincide'.

key_findings.finding: Three-class (low/medium/high) classification from the top-5 voice features gives overall accuracy above the 33% chance rate for most criteria, but not above the 50% majority-class baseline for self-report.
key_findings.numbers: All-cases accuracy (%): Self N 50, E 46, O 46, A 53, C 43. Expert N 57, E 60, O 57, A 56, C 53. Close others N 54, E 57, O 45, A 52, C 54. Chance 33%; a constant central-class prediction gives 50% because the central band holds 50% of cases (p.14).

key_findings.finding: Within-class accuracy is highest for medium-trait cases and lower for low and high cases. Some cells are extreme: the Conscientiousness high-trait cell for self-report is 4.1%.
key_findings.numbers: Medium-trait accuracy ranges 47.4% to 81.1%; examples: close-other Neuroticism medium 76.4%, expert Neuroticism medium 81.1%. Self-report Conscientiousness high 4.1%, Extraversion high 18.2%. Close-other Conscientiousness low 0%, high 64.3%.

key_findings.finding: Expert zero-acquaintance rating reliability was moderate to strong on four dimensions and low on Openness. This rating is the criterion that the authors say voice predicts best.
key_findings.numbers: ICC on N=20 videos: Emotional Adjustment 0.70, Extraversion 0.73, Agreeableness 0.74, Conscientiousness 0.82, Openness 0.23. Experts discussed disagreements and re-rated Openness.

key_findings.finding: The Discussion's numbers do not match the Results. It says the highest trait correlations were Neuroticism 0.38 and Extraversion 0.40, and that the predictions range 0.3 to 0.4. Results and Table 4 report 0.47 to 0.48 for Extraversion.
key_findings.location: Abstract p.1 (lines 45-47); Discussion p.14 (lines 1129-1132); Results p.8-10 (lines 459-460, 466, 475)
key_findings.numbers: Discussion: N 0.38, E 0.40. Results: E 0.47 (self), 0.48 (expert). Text claims all correlations p<0.001 with a maximum of 0.50, but Table 4 shows p = 0.0013, 0.002, 0.004 and 0.01 for some cells and a maximum of 0.48.

key_findings.finding: The authors compare the voice results with facial-expression work and conclude voice alone is more limited; they call personality prediction a multimodal task.
key_findings.numbers: Voice best case about 60% accuracy vs over 75% for facial-expression work by Gavrilescu (ref 56, cited as [56]).

limitations: Sample: 100 participants, all female, mostly psychology students (age 18-27 in Sample 1). Authors say the group is homogeneous in age and personality, so extreme trait values are unlikely, limiting external validity (p.16).
Effect sizes are moderate and may not hold in larger or more varied samples; the authors say they should be read cautiously (p.16).
No cross-cultural sampling; the authors say cultural norms may change how traits are externalized through voice (p.16).

Confounders: noise in some recordings; two different microphones for Sample 1 and Sample 2, which the authors say may explain the lack of replication; colds, fatigue and emotional state could act as latent variables (p.16).
Only vocal aspects were analyzed. Fluency (pauses, discontinuities), morphology/syntax, conversational behavior, facial expression, body language and movement were not (p.17).
Feature interpretability is weak: most top features are MFCC or LPC coefficients whose meaning is unclear, and the top features did not replicate across samples (pp.12-15).

No explicit power analysis. The authors say N = 100 gives 80% power for correlations near 0.2 (p.5, lines 300-304). Many features (1941) raise the risk of spurious correlation; the authors used two samples to check consistency (p.5).
Expert Openness reliability was low (ICC 0.23 on 20 videos) (p.7).

Internal inconsistencies found in the text, not reconciled by the authors: Sample sizes 78 + 44 = 122 vs N = 100; Discussion correlation values (0.38/0.40) vs Results (0.47/0.48); Extraversion close-other r given as both 0.40 and 0.41; 'all p < 0.001' vs Table 4 p-values up to 0.01; 'one of two experts' vs both experts rating videos (p.7).
Data are available only on request for privacy reasons, so the results cannot be reproduced from the paper alone (p.17).

Prediction set-up: the text does not say whether feature selection (top-5 by correlation) was done inside each leave-one-out fold; this must be checked before accepting the 43-60% accuracies as out-of-sample.
measures: Big Five self-report: NEO-FFI, 60-item Spanish adaptation (Cordero et al. 2008), completed in a group session (p.7).

Close-other judgments: 3-point (low/medium/high) rubric for 5 dimensions, completed by a relative or close friend; adapted from the NEO-FFI manual summary sheet (p.7; rubric in Supplementary Materials).

Expert zero-acquaintance ratings: 15 cm visual analog scale per Big Five dimension, scored as cm from the 0 mark, based on watching the full video (p.7). Two experienced PhD assessors (one female, one male; over 25 years of experience); calibrated to 100% agreement on cues before rating.
Inter-rater ICC on 20 videos: Emotional Adjustment 0.70, Extraversion 0.73, Agreeableness 0.74, Conscientiousness 0.82, Openness 0.23 (p.7).
Voice features: OpenSMILE AVEC 2011 emotion set, 1941 functionals (LLDs, deltas, voicing, durations) (p.6, Tables 1-2).
Dependent variable for prediction: low/medium/high classes at training-set 25th and 75th percentiles (p.13).
references_of_note: Ambady and Rosenthal 1992, Psychol. Bull. 111:256 (ref 3): thin-slice meta-analysis, overall accuracy 0.39 in zero-acquaintance predictions of outcomes. Relevant to the persuasion/accuracy theme.

Mairesse, Walker, Mehl and Moore 2007, J. Artif. Intell. Res. 30:457 (ref 14): automatic recognition of personality from linguistic cues in conversation and text. Closest text-measurement precedent in the reference list.
Van Zant and Berger 2020, J. Pers. Soc. Psychol. 118:661 (ref 23): 'How the voice persuades'; paralinguistic cues (pitch, volume) enhance persuasion. Only persuasion-related work the paper cites.
Breil, Osterholz, Nestler and Back 2021 (ref 24): review of 32 studies, up to 39 non-verbal cues, correlations with Big Five traits.
Cannata et al. 2022, Technol. Mind Behav. 3:1 (ref 27): framework linking psychological and AI personality research; the paper's stated bridge.
Hickman et al. 2022, J. Appl. Psychol. 107:1323 (ref 50): reliability, validity and generalizability of automated video-interview personality assessments.
Koutsoumpis et al. 2024, Comput. Hum. Behav. 154:108128 (ref 49): audio signals predict self-report and expert-rated traits in asynchronous video interviews.
Hosoda, Stone-Romero and Coats 2003 (ref 60): meta-analysis of physical attractiveness effects on job outcomes; cited for recruiter attribution bias.
Youyou, Kosinski and Stillwell 2015, PNAS 112:1036 (ref 57): computer-based personality judgments more accurate than human judgments.
Eyben et al. 2010 (ref 39, OpenSMILE) and Schuller et al. 2011 (ref 38, AVEC 2011 feature set): the feature pipeline used.
Mohammadi and Vinciarelli 2012, IEEE Trans. Affect. Comput. 3:273 (ref 41): automatic personality perception from prosodic features; Speaker Personality Corpus source.
Pennebaker and King 1999 (ref 59) and Argamon et al. 2005 (ref 58): lexical and linguistic-style predictors of personality; the text-based tradition the authors contrast with voice.
Marrero et al. 2022, Acta Psychol. 230:103740 (ref 21): voice samples predict self-reported traits (about 10% of variance).

short_quotes.quote: Voice features are related to the externalization of individuals' personality characteristics.

ext.identification: None in the causal sense. The design is cross-sectional: correlations between acoustic features and three personality criteria (Sample 1, with Sample 2 as a replication for self-report), then leave-one-out random-forest classification on N = 100. No instrument, quasi-experiment or manipulation. Out-of-sample validity depends on whether feature selection was inside each fold, which the text does not state.
ext.theory_note: The paper treats personality as externalized through vocal cues and perceived by judges. Accuracy and externalization are kept separate (Brown and Bradshaw 1985).

rel.summary_md:
Rubio, Aguado, Toledano and Fernandez-Gallego (Sensors 2024) recorded about 7-minute mock job interviews with Spanish women, nearly all students. They extracted 1,941 OpenSMILE AVEC-2011 acoustic functionals and correlated them with Big Five scores from three sources: NEO-FFI self-report, close-other ratings and zero-acquaintance expert ratings. In Sample 1 (n=78), the best single feature reached r of about 0.30-0.48 per trait. Expert ratings tracked voice most closely (E 0.48, N -0.47). The paper also says N=100, but its two samples add to 122.

The key result is negative: the top features did not replicate in Sample 2 (n=44). The authors suggest a microphone change may explain this. For prediction, the top five features fed a random forest that sorted people into low, medium or high on each trait, scored by leave-one-out. Self-report accuracy was 43-53%, no better than the 50% you get by always guessing "medium". Expert ratings did best, at 53-60%. The paper never says whether the top five features were chosen inside each fold, so even those figures may be optimistic. The Discussion's numbers also contradict the Results (0.38/0.40 vs 0.47/0.48).

For Melange, the paper backs the audio lane's existing verdict rather than reopening it. The lane uses a related toolkit (eGeMAPS v02 from openSMILE), and its audio Neuroticism (N) pilot was a MISS. Audio is display-only, and the engine never reads it. The paper adds two concrete cautions. First, a change of channel (microphone or venue) can wipe out feature-level findings. Second, a sample of one sex hides the sex confound in pitch variability. Melange measured that confound, but the fix is not on the live branch (see flags).

bearings.paper_claim: Single-feature voice-trait correlations of r about 0.30-0.48 in Sample 1 (n=78) did not replicate in Sample 2 (n=44, self-report only): different top features, which the authors call results that 'did not coincide'. They blame the switch between two microphones, plus noise, colds and fatigue. Voice alone peaks at about 60% three-class accuracy, against over 75% in facial-expression work, so they call personality prediction a multimodal task.
bearings.paper_location: Section 3.1.6, pp.12-13 (lines 981-998); Limitations p.16; Discussion p.14 (lines 1138-1144)
bearings.system_side: The lane extracts eGeMAPS v02 (88 openSMILE functionals) per verified solo clip, pools them per member weighted by duration, then z-scores and winsorizes at +/-5. Channel (studio, remote or telephone) is recorded as uncontrolled. There is a large venue confound in disfluency (about 26 per 1k words live vs 0.22 per 1k on NPR). The engine and ranks never read audio, and the audio N look was spent and MISSed on 2026-08-25.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper's sample is all female, Spanish, mostly aged 18-27, with self-report criteria. Members of Congress are mixed-sex and older, recorded across many outlets, with no self-report criterion. The transfer is the methodological lesson: feature-level findings break when the recording channel changes. The effect sizes do not transfer. The Melange corpus has much more channel heterogeneity than two microphones, so the instability risk is larger here, which reinforces display-only.

bearings.paper_claim: Prediction: the 5 features most correlated with each trait were picked from 1,941, scores were binned at the 25th/75th percentiles, and a random forest (20 trees) was scored by leave-one-out on N=100. Self-report accuracy was N 50, E 46, O 46, A 53, C 43%, against a 50% majority-class baseline. Expert accuracy was 53-60%. The paper does not say whether feature selection ran inside each fold, and it applies no multiple-comparison correction across 1,941 correlations.
bearings.system_side: The audio pilot does no univariate pre-selection. Ridge regression uses all 88 features, alpha is tuned by GridSearch inside each outer fold, and 5-fold CV is repeated over 5 seeds. A permutation null with the same estimator sets the noise floor. The ES cross-modal re-test likewise uses all 88 features with nested CV and 5000 label permutations, and no analyst sign choices. That re-test gave held-out r=+0.208 (perm p=.0002) at the Melange N; it is a single path and stays UNVERIFIED as a trait claim.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Melange's design already guards against the leakage this paper may contain, so Rubio's accuracies cannot be used as a bar or prior for Melange looks. The overall rates sit at or below the 50% majority baseline for self-report, and selection may have run outside the folds. At most they say the expected effect is small: about r 0.3-0.5 for the best single feature, before correcting for selection across 1,941 features. That fits Melange's MISS at N=90.

bearings.paper_claim: All 100 participants are female. The authors list this as a limit on generalization, and it also removes sex as a confound in pitch features. The paper never estimates how sex affects F0-based features.
bearings.system_side: Melange measured r(sex=F)=-0.266 (d=-0.944, 1,324 clips / 309 members) on F0semitone stddevNorm. Commit 4193f0140 changed pitch_variability_raw to the plain semitone SD (stddevNorm*amean) and barred stddevNorm on its own. That commit is NOT an ancestor of HEAD (git merge-base --is-ancestor returns false). The live file still emits stddevNorm alone and labels the metric without the bar.
bearings.transfer_conditions: A same-sex study gives no evidence that pitch-variability effects survive in a mixed-sex legislature. Any pitch-based descriptor in Melange needs sex conditioning or the de-normalized SD. Melange's own Salam-2022 check found pace and volume_dynamics free of sex effects; pitch variability and jitter are not.

bearings.paper_claim: The strongest voice correlates come from zero-acquaintance expert ratings made from video plus audio (E 0.48, N -0.47, C 0.44), not from self-report. The authors read this as voice tracking what a listener attributes more than the person's self-view. Self-other agreement on Openness was not significant, and expert Openness ICC was 0.23.
bearings.paper_location: Table 3-4 pp.8-12; Discussion pp.14-16 (lines 1155-1160, 1225-1228); Section 2.2.2 p.7
bearings.system_side: The persona channel models the projected persona that a lobbyist meets, built from LLM cue classification of text. The audio descriptors are written as listener-facing descriptions in narrative paragraphs and make no trait claims.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This loosely supports framing audio as a perceived persona rather than a trait. The expert-rating result rests on two raters and 20 ICC videos in a non-political, all-female sample, so it does not validate any Melange persona weight. PERSONA_W stays an owner ruling.

gaps_exposed: The sex-confound fix for pitch_variability_raw (stddevNorm*amean, commit 4193f0140, 2026-08-21) is not on the live branch. fec/members/b5_audio_descriptors_candidate.py:217 still emits stddevNorm alone, a metric Melange itself measured as sex-loaded (r=-0.266). This finding is UNVERIFIED under DE-062: one path only (git ancestry plus a file read).

There is no explicit channel or microphone stratum. Rubio's non-replication across two microphones suggests eGeMAPS features should be checked for stability within member across recording channels, or z-scored within venue. The brain lists channel as uncontrolled.

Melange has no test of whether vocal descriptors match how listeners perceive members, as opposed to self-reported traits. That is where Rubio found the strongest signal (expert ratings). The system has no rater panel for audio-perceived persona.
flags: Do not cite Rubio's 43-60% accuracies as evidence that voice predicts personality. For self-report they do not beat the 50% majority baseline. Fold placement of feature selection is unstated. There is no multiple-comparison correction across 1,941 features.

The paper is internally inconsistent: N=100 vs 78+44=122; Discussion r 0.38/0.40 vs Results 0.47/0.48; 'all p<0.001' vs Table 4 p values up to 0.01. Quote figures only from the Results tables, with the sample named.

Every figure comes from a homogeneous Spanish sample of 100 women in mock job interviews, with a recording date not stated. Mark any transfer to members of Congress as UNSTRATIFIED by sex and channel.
The audio N route is closed (look spent 2026-08-25). This paper does not justify reopening it, and a new audio-trait look would need a fresh pre-registration under the single-look discipline.

The missing-fix finding (4193f0140 not an ancestor of HEAD) is new agent analysis and stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062). It is reported here, not repaired: the repo is read-only for this task.
rel.paul_alignment: Paul's notes favor non-textual channels (audio, video, image) and ask for a framework that handles the 'contextual or auditory constraints' of a format (Ramey). Rubio gives that concern concrete content: one microphone change was enough to break feature-level replication, and voice alone reached only about 60% at best. Overall, the evidence sides with the system's conclusion (audio is display-only; the audio N pilot MISSed) more than with an expectation that voice will yield trait scores. Paul's note is not stale so much as left open: it asks for a framework, and the system has answered with display-only plus reliability ranking (pause .92 > pace .86 > volume .85 >> pitch). Paul did not annotate this paper.

related.why: Rubio cites Marrero (ref 21): voice samples explain about 10% of self-reported trait variance. Both test the same voice-to-self-report question, with similarly modest effects.

Same target: automatic recognition of self-reported personality. Melange's Salam-2022 check on sex-clean pace and volume, and on sex-loaded pitch variability, fills in the sex-confound question that Rubio's all-female sample cannot answer.
Audio as data for political research: alignment, features and classification pitfalls. Rubio's non-replication across microphones is a concrete case of those pitfalls.
Vocal pitch in congressional speech measures emotional intensity, not trait. It is the political-domain counterpart to Rubio's lab interview setting.
Expert ratings of legislators' traits (Personality on the Hill) play the same role as Rubio's zero-acquaintance expert criterion, which tracked voice most closely.
Ramey measures elite personality from the words in speech; Rubio measures it from the acoustics. Rubio sets the voice channel against the lexical tradition.
A review of threats in personality computing. Rubio's selection-leakage ambiguity and failed replication are examples of the reproducibility problems it covers.
